classification_signals: Section 1.0 ABSTRACT: 'The existing literature offers relatively strong evidence that characteristics of buildings and indoor environments significantly influence...', 'This paper will consider both direct productivity gains and gains associated with reducing adverse health effects.', 'The economic results of previous analyses were updated to 1996...', 'In two example calculations, the potential financial benefits of improving indoor environments exceed costs by factors of 9 and 14.'

Section 3.0 APPROACH: 'Computer-based literature searches and personal contacts were used to identify relevant papers and the evidence supporting or refuting the hypothesized linkages was synthesized.'

Section 3.0 APPROACH: 'The potential economic significance of adverse health effects linked to the indoor environment was estimated, primarily by synthesizing and updating the results of previously published estimates.'

Section 3.0 APPROACH: 'Nationwide health and productivity gains were then computed by multiplying the potential percentage decrease in illness (or percent direct increase in productivity) by the associated cost of the illness (or by the associated magnitude of the economic activity).'
Tables 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 summarize findings from multiple cited studies, indicating a synthesis of existing research.

The paper explicitly states it 'draws heavily on a previously published paper (Fisk and Rosenfeld 1997)' and updates it with 'new research findings, more recent statistical data, and 1996 prices.' (p. 4).

limitations: Existing data and knowledge are inadequate for precise estimates of potential productivity gains from better indoor environments (Abstract, p. 2).
Only crude estimates of the magnitude of productivity gains can be developed (Abstract, p. 1).
The estimation of the magnitude of decrease in adverse health effects and direct improvements in productivity from improved indoor environments is the most uncertain step (p. 2).
Small studies without sufficient statistical power or those judged to be of poor quality were disregarded (p. 2).
Potential confounding in studies means low ventilation rates or mechanical air recirculation are suspected risk factors but not proven to increase illness transmission (p. 5).
The relative importance of transmission mechanisms for many common respiratory illnesses remains controversial (p. 5).
Only one paper with a null finding regarding building factors and respiratory disease was identified, and it had important methodological limitations (p. 7).
The complexity of disease transmission makes it difficult to estimate the magnitude of practical reduction for the U.S. population (p. 9).
The magnitude of potential reduction in allergy and asthma symptoms is quite uncertain (p. 15).
Quantification of the societal cost of Sick Building Syndrome (SBS) is very difficult (p. 17).
Limited information is available on the influence of SBS symptoms on worker productivity (p. 17).
It is unclear how to translate specific performance test increases/decreases into an overall productivity decrement from SBS symptoms (p. 18).
Some self-reported productivity decrement may be due to factors other than SBS symptoms (p. 18).
Workers dissatisfied with the indoor environment may provide exaggerated estimates of productivity decreases (p. 18).
Research on direct environmental impacts on human performance is difficult due to complexity of defining/measuring performance in real-world environments and multiple influencing factors (p. 20).
Not all studies have found associations between thermal environment and work performance (p. 20).
The potential to use improved lighting to significantly improve office worker performance seems largely unproved (p. 23).
Most research subjects for lighting studies have been young adults, while lighting is expected to have a larger influence on older adults (p. 23).
Odor intensity was uncharacterized in some studies and may have exceeded intensities normally experienced in buildings (p. 23).
Implications of laboratory odor studies for overall worker performance in actual workplaces are not readily quantified (p. 25).
Intentionally exposing workers to chemicals with scents could be considered unethical (p. 25).
Extrapolations from laboratory studies to the real workforce are the only available avenues for estimating productivity gains (p. 25).
Some performance measures used in research may not directly reflect overall productivity changes (p. 25).
Research often focuses on tasks requiring excellent concentration/quick responses/vision, which represent only a fraction of most workers' time (p. 25).
Environmental condition changes in many studies are larger than average changes likely to be made in buildings to improve productivity (p. 25).
Specific and compelling cost-benefit data needed to motivate changes in building codes, designs, and operation/maintenance policies are not yet available (p. 29).
minimum_safe_summary: This systematic review synthesizes existing literature to estimate the potential nationwide productivity and health benefits from improved indoor environments. It updates previous economic analyses to 1996 dollars, projecting annual savings and productivity gains of $40 billion to $250 billion. Key findings include estimated savings of $6-14 billion from reduced respiratory disease, $2-4 billion from reduced allergies and asthma, $15-38 billion from reduced sick building syndrome symptoms, and $20-200 billion from direct improvements in worker performance. Example calculations show financial benefits exceeding costs by factors of 9 and 14. However, the authors acknowledge that existing data and knowledge are inadequate for precise estimates, and many findings are based on extrapolations from laboratory studies or self-reported data, making the magnitude of practical reductions uncertain.
